reasons: Tests in frontend/src/lib/confidence.test.ts cover the derivation and the invalid record branches.
The render test in frontend/src/render.test.tsx checks the same figures on the page.
I did not run these tests in this review.

terms.meaning: the step by step working that turns the inputs into a score
a factor that falls as the sources get older, halving every 540 days
the list stored in a record naming which parts went into its score
how close two numbers must be to count as equal
one stored result, usually a JSON file entry

depends_on: packages/knowledge/confidence.py (the engine this mirrors, referenced in comments, not imported)

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Header and constants for confidence
sections.what: The header sets out the formula and why the viewer recalculates it. It sets the coverage scale, the recency half-life and the tolerance used to decide two scores match.
sections.why: The constants sit in one place so the formula can be read and checked in one spot.
sections.watch_out: The scale and half-life must match the engine, or every recalculated score will disagree.

sections.name: ConfidenceBlock
sections.title: Shape of a confidence record
sections.what: Describes the fields a confidence record must carry, which optional fields fall back to a default, and that the list of contributing features is required with no default.
sections.why: It mirrors the generated contract type so the viewer reads records the same way the producer wrote them.
sections.watch_out: This type is written by hand. When the generated type changes, this one must change too, and a test compares them.

sections.name: Derivation
sections.title: Shape of the derived result
sections.what: Describes what the viewer gets back after working out a record: each factor, the agreement value, the flags, the recalculated score and whether it matches.
sections.why: It gives the pages one place to read each figure, and keeps the stored score separate from the recalculated one.
sections.watch_out: Agreement is null when it was not measured. Code that reads it must not treat null as zero.

sections.name: derive
sections.title: Working out a confidence score
sections.what: Takes one record, works out gaps, effective evidence, coverage and recency, decides from the record whether agreement counts, and returns the recalculated score with a yes or no on whether it matches the stored one.
sections.why: Likely reason: agreement is read from the record rather than guessed from the citation count, because the count could not show when agreement was unmeasured.
sections.watch_out: The invalid record messages are shown to readers, so keep the checks here in step with the schema rules.

sections.name: Standing
sections.title: Three levels of evidence standing
sections.what: Defines the three states a claim can be in: grounded, declared prerequisite, or unsupported.
sections.why: Keeps a claim that depends on enabling work from being shown as fully supported or as having no support at all.
sections.watch_out: A new state must be added to the label table and to the styles, or it will show without a label.

sections.name: standingOf
sections.title: Choosing the standing from citations
sections.what: A claim with at least one citation counts as grounded. A claim with an empty or missing citation list counts as unsupported.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code for why this function never returns the declared prerequisite state.
sections.watch_out: Callers must handle the declared prerequisite state some other way, because this function never returns it.

sections.name: STANDING_LABEL
sections.title: Plain labels for each standing
sections.what: Maps each standing to the words shown on the page. The unsupported state is shown as hypothesis.
sections.why: Keeps the wording in one place so every page says the same thing.
sections.watch_out: The render tests look for some of these words, so changing them breaks those checks.

summary: Turns one stored confidence record into the visible arithmetic that produced its score, and recalculates that score to check it matches.
purpose: Lets the viewer show every step behind a confidence number, and flags any record whose stored score or feature list does not agree with the rules.
why: The header says a bare number hides how it was made, and that a disagreement with the engine should be shown to the reader rather than hidden. Likely reason for recalculating here: to catch drift between this viewer and the engine.
how: Subtracts gaps from the evidence count to get the effective count. Turns that count into coverage, turns source age into a recency factor, reads whether agreement contributed from the record, multiplies the factors together, then compares the result with the stored score within a very small tolerance.
inputs: A confidence block from a record: the stored score, evidence count, load-bearing gaps, mean source age in days, source agreement value, and the list of contributing features.
outputs: A derivation with each factor, the agreement value or null, a flag saying whether agreement was measured, a message if the record is invalid, the recalculated score, and a yes or no on whether it reproduces the stored score. Also a standing label from standingOf and STANDING_LABEL.
risks: The formula is copied from the Python engine, so if either side changes alone the viewer will report a mismatch. A record with no feature list is reported as invalid and not given a default, which is deliberate.
debug: If scores stop reproducing, compare the constants here with the Python engine in packages/knowledge/confidence.py, then check the record's rounding. If an invalid record message appears, check the program that wrote the JSON file.
